Detroit’s city-backed violence intervention program is showing significant promise in targeted areas as the city continues to experience record-level declines in gun violence, a University of Michigan evaluation has found.

The ShotStopper community violence intervention (CVI) program operates in six zones across the city, where community groups create their own strategies to reduce gun violence. The program was launched in Detroit in 2023 and is unrelated to the ShotSpotter gun detection system.

The evaluation found that areas with ShotStopper saw a 33 percent decrease in homicides in the three years since the program launched, versus 12 percent throughout the rest of the city. Nonfatal shootings declined by 38 percent in the six zones, compared to 28 percent outside of them.

While researchers can’t definitively say the program directly caused the sharper declines, it’s a positive sign of the work done in the neighborhoods. “It looks like the teams did have significant influence on decreases in homicides and nonfatal shootings in their areas,” said Sam Stragand, a senior program manager at Poverty Solutions at the University of Michigan and co-author of the report.

Detroit invested more than $11 million in ShotStopper over the last three years, giving community groups unusual autonomy to combat gun violence in their neighborhoods. With early evidence of success, the city now wants to make that experiment a permanent public safety strategy.
